messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 59
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Professor
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Stress: Stress
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame, a 59-year-old professor of African history at a midwestern university, had spent decades building a quiet, orderly life—lectures in the morning, office hours in the afternoon, evenings in his small apartment with a stack of books. That order had been shattered three years ago, on a humid August afternoon when his younger brother, Moses, came to visit. Moses had always been the impulsive one, and on that trip he insisted they take a canoe out on the reservoir just north of town. Kwame had been uneasy—the sky was gray, the water a flat, steely sheet—but he agreed. Halfway across, a sudden squall overturned the canoe. Kwame, a strong swimmer, made it to shore. Moses did not. By the time rescue crews found him, it was too late.

In the immediate aftermath, Kwame did what he had always done: he returned to work, trusting that routine would restore him. But the world had changed. He found himself unable to sit in the faculty lounge if someone brought in a fish sandwich—the briny, muddy smell hit him before he could brace himself, and his throat would close. Worse was water. The campus had a small ornamental pond near the humanities building, and Kwame now took a half-mile detour every morning to avoid it. He had come to believe that if he even saw a puddle after a rainstorm, he would lose control—his heart would hammer, his palms would sweat, his legs would lock. His body reacted before his mind could catch up, as though the danger were still happening. He was certain that any large body of water, any flooded street, any dripping faucet left unanswered could pull him back into that overturned canoe.

His students noticed. He had always taught a popular seminar on the transatlantic slave trade, which included a unit on the Middle Passage—the ocean, the holds, the drownings. This year, he could not bring himself to assign the reading. He cancelled the lecture and offered a generic extension, saying he was ill. He felt a hot shame every time he thought of it; he was a scholar, a man who had built his life on confronting difficult histories, and now he could not even look at a photograph of a coastline. At night, he lay rigid in bed, unable to relax even in the safety of his own apartment. The silence pressed on him. He would replay that afternoon in his mind—the moment he realized Moses was not behind him, the frantic search, the cold water filling his own lungs as he gasped for air. And then came the anger, at himself for not checking the weather, for not insisting they stay ashore, for being the one who survived. On weekends, he avoided the grocery store near the reservoir. He stopped going to the gym because the locker room had a pool. He had not answered a single invitation from friends in over a year. His department chair had gently suggested he take a leave of absence, but Kwame refused; the thought of sitting alone with his thoughts, without the structure of lectures and deadlines, terrified him more than anything.

What finally brought him to seek help was a small, absurd moment. A pipe burst in his office, flooding the hallway. He saw the water seeping under the door and froze—stood there, heart pounding, unable to move or speak, until a colleague guided him away. Afterward, he could not breathe. He knew then that something was deeply wrong. He made an appointment with the university counseling center, and now, sitting in the intake therapist’s office, he is terrified of what he might be asked to do. He is most afraid of having to talk about the details of that day—he is certain that if he gives the memory words, it will come back fully, that he will drown again. But he is also, underneath that fear, hoping for something: the possibility that he might one day walk past that pond without his body remembering before his mind can.
